reader.title: Attempted lynching of Fritz Anschlag
bases: A crowd set out to lynch Anschlag after the bodies were found, pursued the officers and broke into the Anaheim jail to seize him, but did not find him (A2, A4, A8).

A crowd of 'lynchers' acting without authority on a murder accusation tried to seize Anschlag (A2, A4), but no one was killed; the early reports that he (or Decker) was hanged were retracted and contradicted by his later trial (A8, A10, A14).

The Los Angeles Herald, a California AP report and an Anaheim special to the Express independently describe the pursuit and the break-in at the Anaheim jail (A2, A4, A8); the early wire claims of a hanging were corrected the same day (A8, A5).

summary.text: The attempted lynching of Fritz Anschlag took place on the night of January 26-27, 1888, when a crowd from around Garden Grove, California, pursued officers moving Anschlag, a German accused of murdering Charles B. Hitchcock and his wife, and broke into the Anaheim jail to seize him.
Officers had hidden Anschlag and Antoine Decker, a hired man arrested with him, and took both to the Los Angeles county jail the next morning.
Early wire dispatches wrongly reported that he had been hanged.
He was later convicted and sentenced to death, and in November 1888 he poisoned himself in jail.
According to the Los Angeles Herald, Anschlag had agreed to buy Hitchcock's Garden Grove ranch for $8,000 and had been staying with the couple.
After the Hitchcocks disappeared, neighbors searched, and on the afternoon of January 26 a party found both bodies buried on the prairie about three miles from the house.
Anschlag and Decker, a man he had hired at Anaheim, were arrested at the ranch.
Once the bodies were found, "the enraged citizens started out to lynch him," the Herald wrote.
The officers had already left with the prisoners; the first dispatch credited Marshal Insley, the Herald named Constable Finley, and a Sacramento report Constable Farley.
A California Associated Press reporter wrote that "the lynchers" set off from the Hitchcock residence after the officers, reached Anaheim, and broke open the jail, but found no prisoner.
In a thick fog the officers had turned off at the first cross-road and so evaded the crowd.
Accounts differ on where the prisoners spent the night: an Anaheim special to the Los Angeles Express said a store cellar, the Herald a corn-bin, and the Sacramento report the open country.
On the morning of January 27 both men were taken by train to the county jail in Los Angeles.
In jail Anschlag twice confessed to the killings and said Decker had no part in them.
Decker interpreted at the first confession and later testified.
No report of arrests or charges against members of the crowd appears in the coverage.
At his arraignment in Los Angeles on February 6 someone in a crowd outside shouted "Let's hang him," but the Herald judged that the crowd "did not appear to be serious."
A jury found him guilty of first-degree murder on February 18 after sixteen minutes, and Judge Cheney sentenced him to death on February 24.
Due to hang on November 16, he took strychnine in his cell and died early on November 15.

Recalling the case the next day, the Herald wrote that when the crime was discovered "he narrowly escaped lynching at the hands of an infuriated populace," until "better counsel prevailed and the law was left to take its course."

The first Associated Press report, printed in the Herald on January 27 under the deck "The Assassin Lynched by a Posse of Infuriated Citizens," ended with word that the lynching party had overtaken the officers and hanged Anschlag.

Eastern papers ran a shorter wire on January 28 as "A California Lynching" (Wheeling Intelligencer) and "A Fiend's Punishment" (Wheeling Register), saying he "was lynched before officers could interfere."
A Los Angeles dispatch the same day called these accounts incorrect, and the Indianapolis Journal and Carson City's Morning Appeal printed the corrected version.

The correction did not reach every paper: the Emporia Weekly News set the headline "A German Suspected and Lynched for the Crime" above the correction on February 2, and Ohio's Belmont Chronicle reported on February 9 that Anschlag "was lynched at Santa Anna."
The St. Paul Daily Globe headed its report of the confession "The Wrong Man Hung" and stated that "Decker was lynched for the crime," though the Herald placed Decker alive in the jail.
California papers credited the officers who outran the crowd, and the Herald headlined its account "A Disappointed Mob."
The Sacramento Record-Union praised Constable Farley for saving Decker's life while dwelling on the victims' wounds.

At Anschlag's death the Herald reported "expressions of regret that the sentence could not be carried out" and the remark among viewers of his body that "he would have looked better with a rope around his neck."

framing.detail: Eastern papers ran the early wire under 'A California Lynching' and 'A Fiend's Punishment ... Called to Account by Judge Lynch', reporting a hanging that had not happened.
The Sacramento Record-Union praised Constable Farley for saving Decker from the 'lynchers' while dwelling on the victims' wounds and Mrs. Hitchcock's 'pure womanhood'.

The Los Angeles Herald headlined 'A Disappointed Mob' and later wrote that 'better counsel prevailed', yet reported regret that he escaped the gallows and that he 'would have looked better with a rope around his neck'.
The St. Paul Globe headlined 'The Wrong Man Hung', framing the confession as proof vigilantes had lynched an innocent man.

versions.value: Anschlag was overtaken south of Anaheim and hanged
No one was lynched; the crowd broke into the Anaheim jail and found no prisoner, and both men reached the Los Angeles jail

conflicts.note: The no-lynching version is better evidence: it is later, comes from Los Angeles and Anaheim, and is borne out by Decker interpreting in the jail on Jan 27 (A10) and by Anschlag's trial (A14).
Names of the officer who moved the prisoners differ; Finley and Farley may be one man spelled differently.

versions.value: Prisoners kept in the cellar of a store in Anaheim
Anschlag 'it is stated' hidden in a corn-bin
Officers lay out all night in the fog, then reached Anaheim and took the train

J. H. Fritz (Frederick) Anschlag, a German; Antoine Decker, a hired man arrested with him, was also pursued
Anschlag accused of murdering Charles B. Hitchcock and his wife at Garden Grove to gain their ranch; he later confessed
'Enraged citizens', a 'party of lynchers', 'an infuriated populace' of farmers about Garden Grove
